source.title: Scaling Law of Sim2Real Transfer Learning in Expanding Computational Materials Databases for Real-World Predictions
source.authors: Shunya Minami; Yoshihiro Hayashi; Stephen Wu; Kenji Fukumizu; Hiroki Sugisawa; Masashi Ishii; Isao Kuwajima; Kazuya Shiratori; Ryo Yoshida

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether power-law scaling occurs in new settings: materials-property prediction using simulation-to-real and real-to-real transfer learning. It does not test language-model pretraining loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The study measures prediction error as computational-data size changes in materials models. These results bear on V5's extension to transfer-learning settings, but not on language-model cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute scaling, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream language-model tasks.
record.test_reason: It measures held-out prediction error on real materials data while the pretraining or source-data size grows, across fine-tuning, multitask and Real2Real transfer. It fits power laws with an offset (Dn^-α + C). This bears on V5's claim that the power-law form holds in transfer and fine-tuning beyond text pretraining. It does not study language models, parameter or compute scaling, or allocation, so V1–V4, V6 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially right. The authors conclude that in all three case studies, error on real data falls as a power law in computational or source-data size, with strength varying by property and material group. They propose using these curves, and joint simulation–experiment scaling, to size and allocate data generation. They also note that multitask joint scaling departs from the fine-tuning theory.
record.recipe_differences: Uses materials-property regression error (MAE) against simulation-data size in fine-tuning or multitask transfer, rather than language-model cross-entropy against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling differs by property and material class; the authors report slowing or plateauing for CP and thermal conductivity, weak scaling in some polymer classes, and differing scaling according to conformity with the Wiedemann–Franz law. They also report different joint simulation/experimental-data behavior for fine-tuning and multitask learning.

fits_no_version.finding: Marginal rate of substitution between simulated and experimental samples: 221 MD samples equal one experiment for density; 109 COSMO-RS samples equal one experiment for χ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Joint data-size scaling laws can price simulated against real data in transfer learning.

record.code_released: https://github.com/yoshida-lab/MTL ChiParameter (multitask-learning code); other codes available upon reasonable request
record.problems: The study is not about language models or language-model cross-entropy. Some class-level experimental datasets are very small, and the authors warn that apparent non-scalability may not reflect true generalization. The polymer-property prose reports 500 repetitions while the Fig. 1 caption reports 100 trials. The inorganic-transfer prose and Fig. 6 caption differ on which prediction task the plotted MAE represents.
record.rows_left_out: Did not extract the many individual material-level curves in Fig. 6e or separate numeric values from class panels in Fig. 5a; the text provides no individual values for those curves, and the grouped outcomes are recorded in r7–r11. Parity plots and explanatory physical-property comparisons that do not report scaling outcomes were not included.

untested.parts: Only source/simulation data size (and experimental data size) is varied; model size and compute are fixed. There are no image or video models, no repeated-data regime, and no cross-entropy loss (the measure is MAE on regression). Extrapolation of the fits to much larger n is not tested.
Language-model pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation from small to large language-model runs.
Effect of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Downstream language-model task performance vs scale or loss.
Dependence of language-model exponents or splits on fitting choices.

missing.what: Multitask χ joint scaling. Gains from simulation data grow with experimental data size and vice versa (a synergy), unlike the diminishing interaction in Eq. (1); the authors call the 2D Eq. (1) fit invalid. Fitted R(9129, m) = 0.863m^-0.240 + 6.36×10^-16 (the text prints n but means m).
Per-compound scaling curves showing which material species do or do not scale. Metallic groups keep improving after the average plateaus.

record.verdict_notes: This is a non-language-model, non-cross-entropy setting with a fixed model size: only data size is scaled, and fits include an asymptote C. Fitted exponents are very small (0.0145–0.265), so 'power law' here is close to log-linear decay over 2–3 decades. The record has inconsistencies: 500 vs 100 trials in the prose versus captions, and Fig. 6 caption task labels.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Effects of language-model architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests transfer-learning scaling for materials property prediction, not language models, image/video models, repeated-data training, or other modalities and regimes.
Downstream language-model task performance as a function of language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Whether language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on fitting choices, or whether language-model curves bend.

rows.subject: fully connected multi-layer neural network (polymer property predictor)
rows.stage_stated: pretrained on MD data and fine-tuned on experimental data
rows.operation_detail: Vary the number of MD-simulated polymers used for pretraining, then evaluate fine-tuned prediction error.

conditions.value: refractive index
n varied across 10 logarithmically spaced points from 100 to the maximum dataset size; approximately 7×10^4 polymers overall
80% of experimental data for fine-tuning and 20% held out

rows.baseline: Direct learning without pretraining; exact MAE not stated
rows.value: Estimated power law: D = 0.0684, α = 0.0145, C = 1.75 × 10−11; the error decays almost linearly on a logarithmic scale.
rows.note: The prose says the transfer performance notably surpasses direct learning. The text describes 500 repetitions, while the Fig. 1 caption says the plotted average is over 100 trials.

rows.value: Estimated surface: R(n, m) = (0.0192 + 0.338n−0.265) m−0.239 + 0.0535. Both data-size increases reduce error; increasing experimental data gives a larger gain, and the simulation-data scaling effect weakens as m increases.

rows.note: The study reports 500 independent trials for the density scaling analysis.

rows.measure: Average MAE; the Fig. 6 caption identifies this as thermal-conductivity-task MAE
rows.baseline: Direct learning; exact MAE not stated
rows.value: Estimated power law: 1.44n−0.0836 + 8.05 × 10−7; the authors describe performance as improving linearly on a logarithmic scale, with an overall plateau around n = 4 × 10^3.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation and 90% confidence interval by bootstrapping
rows.locator: Results, transfer learning for thermal and electrical conductivity; Fig. 6c
rows.note: The prose describes transfer from thermal to electrical conductivity, but the figure caption describes the plotted MAE as for the thermal-conductivity prediction task.
rows.check: State is correct. The fitted exponent is small (α=0.0836) and the average plateaus around n=4×10^3. The Fig. 6 caption mislabels the axes (thermal vs electrical conductivity task), so it is unclear which task's MAE is plotted.

relationships.condition: Polymer refractive index and density fine-tuning, χ multitask overall and scalable polymer classes, inorganic WF-conforming subset
relationships.reason: Error falls roughly log-linearly with source-data size and is fit by Dn^-α+C. Exponents are very small (e.g., α=0.0145, 0.0348). The density joint surface matches Eq. (1). Rows r1, r2, r5, r6, r7, r10.
relationships.display_finding: Error fitted Dn^−α+C with small exponents including 0.0145 and 0.0348, and the joint density surface matched the proposed expression.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Polymer refractive index and density fine-tuning, χ multitask overall and scalable polymer classes, inorganic WF-conforming subset
source_check.reason: r1, r2, r5 and r6 report power-law fits or log-linear error decay; r7 and r10 report strong scaling in the named subsets.

relationships.condition: Properties with noisy or biased simulations (CP, thermal conductivity) and the inorganic overall average
relationships.reason: Decay slows after n≈10^4 for CP, plateaus for thermal conductivity, and the inorganic average plateaus near n=4×10^3, so a single power law fits only part of the range (r3, r4, r9).
relationships.display_finding: Decay slowed after about 10^4 simulations for CP, thermal conductivity plateaued, and the inorganic average saturated near 4×10^3.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Properties with noisy or biased simulations (CP, thermal conductivity) and the inorganic overall average
source_check.reason: r3, r4 and r9 show weaker or saturating improvement relative to other settings. However, plateaus alone do not establish failure of an offset power law; the reason's assertion that only part of the range fits is stronger than the text establishes.

relationships.condition: Source–target pairs with weak physical relatedness (non-WF compounds; some polymer classes)
relationships.reason: No improvement with more source data for non-WF compounds (r11) or for polyacrylamide-type classes (r8). The class results are caveated by tiny test sets.
relationships.display_finding: Additional source data produced no improvement for non-WF compounds and almost none for polyacrylamide-type classes, whose test sets were very small.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Source–target pairs with weak physical relatedness (non-WF compounds; some polymer classes)
source_check.reason: r8 reports almost no improvement and r11 explicitly reports no improvement as source data increase; absent effects require challenges for these condition groups. Polymer-class evidence remains tentative because samples are small, and weak physical relatedness is not established as its sole explanation.

relationships.condition: Joint simulation × experimental data scaling under multitask learning
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not a row: the multitask n–m interaction contradicts Eq. (1), and the authors call the Eq. (1) fit invalid there.
relationships.display_finding: Multitask simulation–experiment interactions invalidated the separable joint fit while retaining individual power-law curves.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Joint simulation × experimental data scaling under multitask learning
source_check.reason: The p. 9 results invalidate the specific separable joint surface in Eq. (1), while retaining individual power-law scaling curves. V5 does not specify that joint interaction or separability, so this finding alone does not limit its stated power-law-form claim.

reader_labels.reason: Reported power-law or near-log-linear error scaling in refractive index, density, χ prediction, and inorganic conductivity transfer (r1, r2, r5, r6, r9).
